I feel happy to present otorhinolaryngological fraternity of the country, the first otorhino­laryngology 
(ENT) textbook, which is based on the new Competency-based Medical Education (CBME) ENT 
Curriculum 2019 for Indian Medical Graduate (IMG). It is developed and implemented by National 
Medical Commission (NMC) erstwhile Medical Council of India (MCI). This third edition of “Diseases of 
Ear, Nose and Throat” presents the knowledge of diseases of ear, nose and throat in a concise format. 
The didactic presentation will make this textbook attractive to the medical students, residents and 
practitioners. I am grateful to the students and teachers for their feedback on its first and second 
editions and that facilitated the development of this third edition.

When I started working for this third edition, I knew that it would be a challenge to organize 
the content in the format of new medical curriculum for undergraduates in consonance with 
the changing health needs of the country. I have strived to maintain the international standards. The new Graduate Medical 
Education Regulations (GMR/GMER 2019) intends to take the IMG to provide health care to the evolving needs of the nation 
and the world. As the IMG is supposed to provide preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and holistic care to his patients, this 
edition has a section on community medicine. I have tried my best to enunciate clearly the competencies that students must 
be imparted.

The thrust in GMER (2019) is on making medical education more learner-centric, patient-centric, gender sensitive, outcome-
oriented and environment appropriate. As the student should be able to effectively communicate with patients and their 
relatives, the textbook has a section on AETCOM (Attitude, Ethics and Communication). It gives me great satisfaction to state 
that this  “competency-based otorhinolaryngology undergraduate textbook” has been prepared keeping in mind the NMC/
MCI’s vision of creating a competent IMG to serve the community. Wherever felt necessary, the “broad subject competencies” 
have been split into “sub-competencies”. Keeping in mind the “patient centric curriculum”, case studies are incorporated in the 
chapters liberally. Even the first year students can read the Anatomy and Physiology of Ear, Nose, Throat, Head and Neck from 
this book because keeping in mind the “early clinical exposure”, plenty of case studies are given in the Anatomy and Physiology 
chapters.

As the skill acquisition is an indispensable component of medical education, a separate section on required skill has been 
kept in the book. The highest level of skill acquisition is a “show how” (SH) in a simulated or guided environment. For few skills 
requiring independent performance (P) and certification, students will get opportunity during their internship.

As per the new curriculum, new chapters have been added which were hitherto not seen in the ENT textbooks while some 
of the chapters usually seen in the ENT textbooks have not been included.

The textbook offers a balanced presentation of contents and emphasizes on the practical aspects of clinical diagnosis and 
patient management. I hope that this ENT textbook will become an important guide to ENT specialty for the students, trainees, 
and the specialists.

I would like to acknowledge my parents, late Shri Ramchandra Bansal and Smt Kalawati Devi Bansal, for enabling me to 
survive comfortably during my seemingly endless years of education. My family has unswervingly endorsed the time required 
for this task, so heartfelt love and thanks go to my wife, Sushma, as well as our children Mohit and Tejal, their spouses (Astha and 
Kushal) and their kids (Agastyaa and Meivaan).

MIDDLE EAR

The middle ear cleft (Fig. 8), which is lined by mucous membrane 
and filled with air, consists of the middle ear, Eustachian tube, 
aditus ad antrum, mastoid antrum and mastoid air cells. Middle 
ear is a 1–2 cm3 air-filled cavity that houses ossicles (malleus, 
incus, stapes), muscles (tensor tympani, stapedius) and nerves 
(chorda tympani, tympanic plexus).
Parts of Middle Ear (Tympanum)

The dimensions of middle ear are shown in Figure 9. The 
tympanum (Fig. 10) is traditionally divided into three parts—
mesotympanum, epitympanum and hypotympanum.

Mesotympanum: This is the portion of middle ear that 

lies at the level of pars tensa.

Epitympanum (attic): This is the portion of middle ear that 
lies above the level of pars tensa and medial to Shrapnell’s 
membrane and the bony lateral attic wall.

Hypotympanum: This is the portion of middle ear that lies 
below the level of pars tensa. 
 Protympanum: The portion of middle ear around the

Critical Thinking Case and Questions

Case Study 4
A 10-year-young boy is brought into the casualty for severe 
headache, nausea, and fever. The boy was in good health until a 
week ago. He has been suffering from right ear purulent, putrid 
and continuous discharge for about an year. Bright lights seem 
to bother him. He appears lethargic and ill. His temperature is 
102°F. Movements of the neck are painful. Otoscopic examination 
revealed right ear CSOM with cholesteatoma. The heart and lung 
examinations are normal. The boy refuses to flex his head because 
that worsens the pain. His general appearance is that of sepsis. See 
Chapter 35 “Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media and Cholesteatoma”.
Questions:
1.  What is the most probable diagnosis?
2.  What could be the anatomical explanation of the symptoms?
Answers are given at the end of chapter.

OBJECTIVE
Describe the boundaries of middle ear (AN 40.2.1).
Boundaries of Middle Ear (Fig. 11)

Middle ear has six boundaries: roof, floor, medial, lateral, 
anterior and posterior walls.

Roof (tegmental wall): It is formed by tegmen tympani 
(a thin plate of bone), which extends posteriorly to form 
the roof of the aditus and antrum (tegmen antri). Tegmen 
tympani separates middle ear from the middle cranial fossa.

be congenitally dehiscent. In such cases, jugular bulb projects 
into the middle ear and is at greater risk of injury during surgery

middle ear mucosa.

PHYSIOLOGY OF HEARING

The pinna collects sound signal1 from the environment, 
which passes through EAC and vibrates the TM (Fig. 29). 
Vibrations of the TM are transmitted to the stapes footplate 
through the chain of ossicles.2 Vibrations of stapes footplate 
result in the pressure changes in the labyrinthine fluids3 

that lead to movement of the basilar membrane and thus 
stimulate the hair cells of the organ of Corti. The IHC of cochlea 
act as transducers and convert the mechanical energy into 
electrical impulses which travel along the auditory nerve.

Clinical Highlights and Additional Important Points

Pinna has to be pulled upward, backward and laterally to see the TM in adults. It attains 90–95% of adult size by 5–6 
years of life.

Auricular cartilage: It gives shape to pinna and is absent in the lobule. Dehiscences may be seen in outer cartilaginous 
ear canal.
Foramen of Huschke: It lies in the vicinity of the “fissure of Santorini”.

External auditory canal: It is smaller than Eustachian tube and is 24 mm in length. Outer one-third (8 mm) is cartilaginous 
and inner two-thirds (16 mm) is bony. Bony EAC does not contain ceruminous glands or hair follicles. The pH is acidic in 
normal healthy ear canals.
Red TM may be normal in a crying child.
Retracted TM shows prominent lateral process of malleus and foreshortened handle of malleus.
Bulging TM loses all landmarks.

Tympanic membrane: It develops from all the three germinal layers: ectoderm (outer epithelial layer), mesoderm (middle 
fibrous layer) and endoderm (inner mucosal layer).

Dimensions of middle ear: Vertical and anteroposterior dimensions are 15 mm each. Transverse dimension is 2 mm in 
mesotympanum (narrowest between the umbo and promontory), 6 mm in epitympanum and 4 mm in hypotympanum.
Tegmen tympani: Plate of bone separating attic of middle ear from middle cranial fossa.

Ossicles: Malleus and incus are derived from Meckel’s cartilage of the first branchial (pharyngeal) arch. Stapes 
superstructure and styloid process develop from Reichert’s cartilage of second branchial arch. Stapes footplate and 
annular ligament are derived from the otic capsule.

Stapes: It is the smallest bone of body and weighs about 2.5 mg. Stapes footplate covers oval window. Area of stapes 
footplate is 3.2 sq mm.
Stapedius muscle: It is supplied by CN VII. Its paralysis causes hyperacusis (phonophobia).

and lateral malleal ligament (superiorly). Posteriorly, it opens into epitympanum.
